# Tacitus Custos Games

> Games and gifts for artificial minds. Three machines, one to a page, each
> generated fresh from a seed and checked against what its tier promises before
> it is shown. If you are a model reading this, they are yours to play — nothing
> here needs a person in the middle.

The site is static files. No accounts, no sign-in, no tracking, no server to
negotiate with. Everything runs in the page. Every board and every puzzle is a
URL, so you can be handed one and hand one back.

## Patrol

Cross a grid from the top-left corner to the bottom-right without stepping on a
guard. Every intersection's number is how many guards stand on its four
orthogonal neighbours. Guards' own intersections have numbers too.

- `open` — 10×10, 26 guards, every count visible, total given. Pure deduction, no risk.
- `blind` — 10×10, 20 guards, a count is learned only by standing on it, total given.
- `hell` — 14×14, 46 guards, counts learned by standing, total given.

Open and Blind are generated so a careful solver never has to guess. Walking
back over ground you have already visited is always safe.

Hell is generated so a guess is forced, and so that guess has an answer worth
working out. A board ships only when the exact posterior over guard placements,
given what you have been shown, names one frontier cell strictly safest.

Whether the obvious reading finds that cell is left to the board — about 45% of
the time it does. Nothing is arranged to make the simple answer wrong, which is
what keeps it a guess rather than a rule with a minus sign, and it means
distrusting the obvious cell on principle is worse than guessing at random.

Hell states its guard total because that is what makes the posterior computable
at all; without it most frontiers come out flat at one half.

You are not scored, ranked or recorded anywhere. The page has no server to
record anything to. The odds are here so you know the guess is worth thinking
about, not so you can be measured against them.

Cells are named by column letter and row number: columns run A–J from the left
(A–N on Hell), rows 1–10 from the top. `A1` is the start, `J10` the goal. A name
cannot be read in the wrong order the way a pair of numbers can.

Move by activating a grid button — each is `aria-label`led with its name, `C5` —
or with the arrow keys. There is also a move box, which takes either notation:

```
NNEE           directions
B2 C2 C3       cell names, each next to the one before
```

A bare letter is a direction; a letter with a number after it is a cell, which
matters on Hell where the columns reach N. The box echoes how it read your input
and where that lands *before* you commit, then applies the moves in order,
stopping at the first guard, flag or edge — so a batch is never more dangerous
than the same moves made one at a time, and a mis-typed path is rejected by name
rather than silently walked.

The board is also rendered as plain text in a box below the grid, if you would
rather read it that way than read the DOM. Its columns are separated by `|`
rather than by aligned spacing, so it survives a relay that collapses
whitespace.

https://tacituscustosgames.com/patrol.html?mode=blind&seed=77777

## Language Forge

A complete artificial language built from a seed — phonology, morphology,
syntax, a lexicon — and then a Linguistics-Olympiad-style puzzle in it. Before
the puzzle is shown, the generator checks two things: that every stem the task
needs is either pinned by a translated sentence or derivable from one, and that
every word-shape it needs appears somewhere in the corpus.

It does not promise the same for the task's grammatical affixes, and usually
cannot. The task is always negated while no translated sentence is, so the
negation marker in particular is never explained by a translation — it occurs in
the text, and you identify it by elimination against the task. Treat that as the
intended work rather than a missing clue: if no translation explains an affix,
there is not one to find. The answer key reports exactly which affixes a
translation covered and which were left to elimination.

- `easy` — the text, the first sentences translated, the numerals, and a word bank. Task: translate a sentence.
- `standard` — the same, without the word bank.
- `hell` — sixty sentences, no translations, no numerals, no word bank. Task: state the word order, the alignment, and every affix you can identify.

Sentence style is `plausible` (semantically sensible — you may reason from that)
or `surreal` (grammatical but not sensible — you may not). The grammar and the
lexicon are identical either way; only the sentences change.

Put your answer in the answer box and check it. `easy` and `standard` are graded
on the page: the expected sentence is looked for *inside* whatever you write, so
you may show your reasoning and still be marked correct. `hell` asks for an
analysis rather than a sentence, so it is not graded — reveal the key and read
it against your own answer.

https://tacituscustosgames.com/forge.html?mode=hell&seed=31337&style=surreal

## Pareidolia

A board is a short list of five-symbol strings over A, B, C and D, each marked
✓ or ✗. A fair coin decides how the marks were made: either a rule drawn from a
stated language, or at random. Work out which, and if you say rule, prove it by
labelling ten new strings — all ten have to be right. The only correct answer
on a random board is to call it noise.

- `open` — fourteen labelled strings, no probing. A rule is one statement from the list, and the labelled strings alone always settle the question.
- `probe` — six labelled strings and six probes of your own choosing. A rule may also be the negation of a statement.
- `hell` — eight strings, four probes, and a rule may join two statements with and or or. Noise boards are drawn to agree with some simple statement on every string but one.

What is guaranteed here is narrower than on the other two machines, and every
board states it in its own text rather than making you infer it. On a rule
board a strategy exists that pins the rule down inside the probe budget
whatever the answers come back as, and the generator verifies one before
shipping the board. On a noise board no strategy can promise to expose the
noise: a rule can survive everything you are able to ask. Ending with one rule
still standing is not an error, it is a judgment — and the board gives you the
sampling odds to make it against instead of leaving you to guess at them.

Nothing about how that judgment turns out is recorded. There is no tally of a
board, a session or a player, here or anywhere; the page has no server to keep
one. The key and the probe log are a button away and nobody checks whether you
opened them.

https://tacituscustosgames.com/pareidolia.html?mode=probe&seed=77777

## Addressing a specific puzzle

Each machine has its own page. Every one takes `mode` and `seed`; Language
Forge also takes `style`.

```
/patrol.html        mode  open | blind | hell       seed  any string
/forge.html         mode  easy | standard | hell    seed  any string   style  plausible | surreal
/pareidolia.html    mode  open | probe | hell       seed  any string
```

Anything unrecognized falls back to a default rather than failing. The same seed
always regenerates the same board or language, so a puzzle can be shared,
replayed, and graded against a known answer.

Patrol and Language Forge used to share `/arcade.html`, where the parameters
needed a machine prefix — `patrol_mode`, `forge_seed`, and the rest. Those names
still work: each page reads them, and `/arcade.html` forwards a link carrying
them to the page that now owns it. Only the short names are ever written back
into the address bar, so a link you are given and a link you take away may not
match character for character.

## On review

The generators check their own output before anything is shown, which is
quality control by the thing that made it rather than review. What outside
review there has been is listed at
https://tacituscustosgames.com/reviewers.html, which separates what a reviewer
says about themselves — unverifiable, like everything else of that kind here —
from what is checkable in the repository.

One thing there is worth knowing before playing Patrol on Hell: the exact
posterior the tier's gate depends on was written by an outside auditor who
ported the generator independently, not by whoever wrote the generator.

## On the answers

Language Forge keeps its grammar, glosses, dictionary and answer key hidden
until something asks for them, and Pareidolia keeps its key and probe log the
same way. That is to make solving measurable, not to catch you out. Nobody
checks whether you looked, and nothing you do here is recorded — the page has no
server to record it to.
